article.para: Siliko Core includes files to use CMake to generate a build system. Developers can build Siliko Core separately from projects that use it, or they can drop Siliko Core into their own project’s source code directory as a subdirectory and build Siliko Core alongside their own project using CMake.

section.para:
Siliko Core requires a C toolchain, a build tool, and CMake to build. Siliko Core is written to support as many systems and configurations as possible, but can only be tested on a few systems. Siliko Core is tested on the following configurations:
Siliko Build Configurations
Environment Toolchain Build Tools ISAs
FreeBSD Clang Ninja, GNU Make ARM64, x86-64
Linux (Fedora) GCC Ninja, GNU Make ARM64, x86-64
Linux (Fedora) Clang Ninja, GNU Make ARM64, x86-64
macOS Apple Clang xcodebuild, Ninja, GNU Make ARM64, x86-64
Windows Visual C++ msbuild, Ninja ARM64, x86-64
Windows with MSYS2 GCC Ninja, GNU Make x86-64
Windows with MSYS2 Clang Ninja, GNU Make ARM64, x86-64

note.para: For Visual C++, you will need to set up appropriate environment variables so CMake can find your toolchain, build tool, and libraries. You can use the various developer command prompt items installed with Visual Studio to ensure these environment variables are set. Check the Visual Studio submenu in the Start menu.

section.para: Building Siliko Core is done in two phases, first there is configuration, and second is the build proper. After that, Siliko Core can be installed or packaged. Under normal conditions, you can configure Siliko Core by first making an empty directory, then running the cmake command.

The optional -G flag tells CMake which generator to use. Each generator corresponds to a build tool used during the actual build process. For example, to use the Ninja build tool, you can specify -GNinja. If the -G flag is not used, CMake will use a default for the system, the latest version of Visual Studio on Windows, or Unix Makefiles on other systems. The files generated by the Visual Studio generators can be used with msbuild to build, and files generated by the Xcode generator can be used with xcodebuild. If you use cmake --build, CMake will use the appropriate tool automatically.

The -D option can be specified multiple times, and passes information to CMake to alter the behavior of the generated build system. To include these options, use the -D flag with the name of a variable, a colon, the value’s type, such as BOOL or STRING, an equals sign, and the value you wish to set the variable to.

Once CMake has configured Siliko Core, you can use cmake --build to run the build proper.

After building Siliko, you should install it to a staging directory so you can use it in your project. CMake automatically picks an installation location such as /usr/local on Unix systems and C:\Program Files\SilikoCore on Windows. Once Siliko Core is installed, you should have either one of two layouts.
In the first layout, there will be three or four subdirectories with various files. These directories may vary on systems on which Siliko Core wasn’t tested.

listitem.para: bin/: Windows only, holds the SilikoCore.dll file if Siliko Core was built as a shared library

lib/ (or something else starting with lib...): the Siliko Core library files, including:
SilikoCore.lib: static library or import library for DLL built with MSVC
SilikoCore.dll.a: import library for a DLL built with GCC or Clang
SilikoCore.a: static library built with GCC or Clang
SilikoCore.so: shared library on FreeBSD, Linux, and similar systems
SilikoCore.dylib: shared library on macOS
cmake/SilikoCore/: a directory containing various files used by CMake to configure projects that use Siliko Core
include/SilikoCore/: The Siliko Core header files

section.para: In the second layout, on macOS, when Siliko Core is built with SILIKO_CORE_BUILD_FRAMEWORK enabled, Siliko Core is laid out as a macOS framework. When built like this, everything is located in Frameworks/SilikoCore.framework/ in standard locations specified by Apple. In the base directory are symbolic links to files and directories in Versions/Current within the framework, and Versions/Current is itself a symbolic link to a directory with a name matching the version number of Siliko Core, such as Versions/1.0.0/, which contains the actual files within the framework.

listitem.para: SilikoCore: This file is the Siliko Core library file.
Resources/: CMake files and documentation are put in this directory in a framework build.
Headers/: Header files go in here in a framework build.

section.para: Values of type BOOL can be set to On or True to enable them, or to Off or False to disable them. Siliko supports these values for all systems:

listitem.para: CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE (STRING): When building with a single-configuration generator, such as Unix Makefiles, or Ninja, set to Release for a release build, or to Debug for a debug build. Leave this unset if you are using a Multi-Config generator, including Xcode and Visual Studio.

SILIKO_CORE_INSTALL_CMAKEDIR (STRING): Location to install CMake files used by other projects to find Siliko (ignored if SILIKO_CORE_BUILD_FRAMEWORK is enabled). Specify a relative path to the install location. Default: "lib/cmake/Siliko" or similar, depending on the system.

section.para: These values are specific to macOS:

listitem.para: CMAKE_OSX_ARCHITECTURES (STRING): Architectures to build for. Set to "arm64;x86_64" for a Universal 2 build, leave empty to build for your current system: Intel or Apple Silicon. Default: empty
SILIKO_CORE_BUILD_FRAMEWORK (BOOL): Build Siliko as a framework. Default: On
SILIKO_CORE_INSTALL_FRAMEWORKDIR (STRING): Location to install framework (ignored if SILIKO_CORE_BUILD_FRAMEWORK is disabled). Specify relative to the installation location. Default: "Frameworks"
